title: Arrays and Linked Lists
description: Compare arrays and linked lists: their internal layouts, performance trade-offs, and when to choose one over the other.

data.text: Arrays and linked lists are the two most fundamental linear data structures. Every other structure you will learn builds on the ideas introduced here: how memory is laid out, how items are accessed, and how insertions and deletions change the cost of an operation.
This lesson explains both structures at a conceptual level, shows how they behave under different workloads, and gives you practical code so you can see the difference for yourself.
An array stores elements in consecutive memory locations. Because the address of each element can be calculated directly from its index, reading an element by position is extremely fast.

data.title: Array characteristics
items: O(n) insertion or deletion in the middle because elements must shift.
Fixed size in low-level languages; dynamic resizing in higher-level languages.

data.title: Array in JavaScript
data.content: A simple array declaration and element access.

data.text: A linked list stores elements as nodes. Each node holds a value and a reference (pointer) to the next node. Because nodes can live anywhere in memory, the list can grow without requiring a large contiguous block.

data.title: Linked list characteristics
items: Nodes are scattered in memory and linked together.
O(n) random access because you must traverse from the head.
O(1) insertion or deletion at the head when the node reference is already known.
Extra memory per node for the pointer.

cards.title: Arrays
cards.description: Best when you know the size upfront or need fast lookups by position.

cards.title: Linked Lists
cards.description: Best when you insert or delete frequently at the front or middle without random access.
pros: Cheap insertions and deletions at known positions.

data.title: Rule of thumb
data.text: If you mostly read by index, choose an array. If you mostly insert or delete at the front or in the middle and do not need random access, a linked list is a better fit. Most production code defaults to arrays or dynamic arrays because their cache performance is hard to beat.

A doubly linked list adds a previous pointer to each node, which makes deletions from the middle O(1) once you have the node, but uses more memory. A circular linked list connects the tail back to the head, which is useful for round-robin scheduling and some game loops.

data.title: Patterns that rely on arrays or linked lists
items: Two-pointer technique on arrays for palindrome checks or pair sums.
Slow-and-fast pointers on linked lists to detect cycles.
Merging two sorted arrays or linked lists.
Reversing a linked list in place with O(1) extra space.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Arrays provide O(1) index access but expensive middle insertions.
Linked lists provide cheap head insertions but O(n) search.
Cache locality makes arrays faster in practice for most workloads.
Choose the structure that matches your dominant operation.
data.takeaway: Mastering arrays and linked lists is the foundation for understanding every more complex data structure that follows.
